native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Across the only three wealth waves available in this file - 1985, 1990 and 1996 - with 1985 the earliest wealth measurement, so "from 1985 onwards" is bounded by these three waves, respondents in the white cohort (racial/ethnic cohort 3 = NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC, a label that also contains the small Asian, Native American and other groups NLSY79 does not separate) held higher median family net wealth than black (cohort 1) and Hispanic (cohort 2) respondents at every wave, and the gap widened substantially in both absolute and relative terms. In nominal dollars exactly as recorded: in 1985 the white median was $3,500 versus $1,600 for black respondents (gap $1,900; ratio 2.2x) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (gap $3,000; ratio 7.0x, a figure to read only with caution because that median is below $1,000 and 41.9% of Hispanic respondents were at or below zero net wealth, so the level gap is the reliable statement); in 1990 the white median was $12,972 versus $4,800 for black respondents (gap $8,172; 2.7x) and $1,600 for Hispanic respondents (gap $11,372; 8.1x); in 1996 the white median was $42,600 versus $9,800 for black respondents (gap $32,800; 4.4x) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (gap $40,038; 16.6x). The white-to-black ratio roughly doubled (2.2 to 4.4) and the white-to-Hispanic ratio rose from about 7 to about 17, and the widening is not an artefact of inflation: in constant 1996 dollars (deflators from CPI-U annual averages, 1982-84=100, with 1985=107.6, 1990=130.7, 1996=156.9, i.e. x1.458 and x1.200) the white-black gap grew from about $2,771 to $32,800 and the white-Hispanic gap from about $4,375 to $40,038, because real median wealth rose about 8.4-fold for whites versus 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics. The ordering white > black > Hispanic is stable at all three waves, but the distributions overlap heavily - in 1996 the white 25th percentile ($8,500) sits below the black median ($9,800) - so the difference is a shift in central tendency and in the share holding no or negative net wealth (1996: 10.9% white, 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic) rather than a clean separation between groups, and the same pattern holds in the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves (1996 ratios 4.7 and 17.8), so it is not produced by available-case estimation. This comparison is purely descriptive and is materially qualified because the wealth variables are a family-level measure (respondent/spouse assets minus debts) assigned to individual respondents who were only 20-28 years old in 1985, so part of the early gap may reflect differences in family formation and marriage rather than individual wealth accumulation, and because all estimates are unweighted and computed on all cases available per wave, with the balanced-panel figures serving as the sensitivity check.
